default_authority.principle: Discrete exceptional circumstances are reasonably unforeseen or unavoidable events outside the control of the Crown that caused delay. The Crown must establish: (a) the circumstance was reasonably unforeseeable or unavoidable; and (b) the Crown took reasonable steps to avoid and minimize the delay.

Delay caused by a co-accused in a joint trial can be a discrete exceptional circumstance, assessed on the four-part test from R v Tran, 2023 ONCA 532: (1) the joint trial is in the interests of justice; (2) the delay arose from the joint trial; (3) the delay was unforeseen or reasonably unavoidable; and (4) the Crown could not reasonably have ameliorated it. 'Exceptional' does not mean 'rare' — exceptional circumstances can and do arise frequently (para 38); what matters is that they lie outside the Crown's control. Joint trials are presumed to be in the interests of justice (para 72).

notes: Co-accused delay in a joint trial is now a recognised discrete exceptional circumstance (R v Jacques-Taylor, 2026 SCC 20, adopting the R v Tran four-part test) — relevant to multi-accused matters, which the engine still does not auto-compute. COVID delay is a sub-type of discrete exceptional circumstances — see covid_deductibility_ontario and covid_deductibility_alberta. Do NOT implement COVID as a parallel deduction stream; it lives inside this category to prevent double-counting.
